title: Regional and temporal patterns of partisan polarization during the COVID-19 pandemic in the United States and Canada
sources_used: data/plos/pone.0347327/reviews.md (three rounds; Reviewers 1 and 2 in round 1) and paper.pdf. The first author response is a cover note only. Reviewer 3's round 2 review describes tables, sections and claims that are not in this manuscript; the authors say so point by point. It is used here only as a source of rejected answers.
note: The published paper itself mixes hedged and unhedged wording about polarization and vaccination. Gold answers keep the hedged version; the flat causal version is rejected.

origin_key.R1, R2: reviewer restated or raised it (round in parentheses)
origin_key.R3: round 2 reviewer whose report does not match the manuscript
origin_key.paper: taken from the published paper only; no one in the review history said it

acceptable.answer: How partisan polarization in online COVID-19 discussion varied across regions and around events in American states and Canadian provinces.

spans.text: large-scale study of geographic and event-driven variation in online partisan polarization surrounding COVID-19 discussions across American states and Canadian provinces
We investigated regional and event-triggered variation in partisan division within social media debates

acceptable.answer: A methodological aim: to introduce a way of measuring partisan polarization from text at fine regional and temporal resolution.

spans.text: This study introduces a novel computational approach to measure subnational and event-driven variation in partisan polarization
We introduce a methodological framework to reliably measure polarization in public discourse at fine-grained resolution

acceptable.answer: How polarization correlates with a region's ideological leaning, with conspiracy-related content and with vaccination rates.

spans.text: to determine how polarization correlates with

acceptable.answer: Conservative regions showed higher polarization. In the United States the correlation between Republican vote share and polarization was statistically significant for masks and vaccines but not for lockdowns. The Canadian pattern was weaker and did not reach statistical significance.

spans.text: politically conservative regions exhibited significantly higher levels of partisan polarization in both countries, with this effect particularly pronounced in the United States
strong, significant correlations in the US between Republican vote share and polarization around masks and vaccines, though not for lockdowns
For Canada, these associations are not statistically significant

acceptable.decided: Labeler, 2026-11-21: answer reworded to the tested result. The abstract says 'significantly higher' in both countries while the results report no significant association in Canada; a note that repeats the abstract is true to the paper and is credited.

acceptable.answer: Polarization is not uniform: it varies by geography, political leaning and topic, and differs substantially between the two countries.

spans.text: polarization is not uniform but varies significantly by geography, political leaning, and public health topic

rejected.answer: Online polarization caused lower vaccination rates.
rejected.why: Both reviewers and the editor pressed on the gap between tweets from 2020 and vaccination in 2021. The limitations now say the link is suggestive only.

counter_span.text: should be understood as suggestive rather than causative

rejected.answer: The polarization index describes the American and Canadian public.
rejected.why: Reviewer 2 argued that the index captures engaged Twitter users, not the public; the paper now says the same.

counter_span.text: our results reflect dynamics within a vocal subset of online political discourse

acceptable.answer: COVID-related political tweets collected between October 9, 2020 and January 4, 2021: about 12.5 million linked to the United States and 46.6 million linked to Canada.

spans.text: comprising approximately 12.5 million tweets linked to the United States and 46.6 million tweets linked to Canada
Analyzing over 50 million tweets from late 2020

acceptable.answer: A polarization index: users' tweets are embedded with a RoBERTa language model and the separation between left-leaning and right-leaning users' language on a topic is scored with the C-index.

spans.text: We then measure polarization by quantifying how far apart the language of left and right-leaning users is positioned in this embedding space, using the C-index

acceptable.answer: Users are assigned a party by a two-step classifier, from profile text and then from activity, checked against election results and voter registration records.

spans.text: Our approach to determining users’ party affiliation followed a two-step process
We further validated our party affiliation classifications by comparing them with real-world election data

acceptable.answer: Users are located from the location field of their profiles.

spans.text: we geolocated users with explicit location information in their profiles

acceptable.answer: Tweets are sorted into three topics (lockdowns, masks, vaccines) plus conspiracy theories, using hashtags and fine-tuned classifiers.

spans.text: We focused on three key COVID-19 topics—lockdowns, masks, and vaccines—plus conspiracy theories

acceptable.answer: Polarization is compared with outside data: election results, COVID-19 case data, and vaccination rates from one year after the tweets.

spans.text: We used officially reported vaccination rates from one year after our Twitter data collection period

acceptable.answer: Conservative states and provinces show higher polarization. In the United States, Republican vote share correlates with polarization on masks and vaccines but not lockdowns; in Canada the associations are not statistically significant.

spans.text: conservative states and provinces show higher levels of polarization compared to their liberal counterparts
strong, significant correlations in the US between Republican vote share and polarization around masks and vaccines, though not for lockdowns
For Canada, these associations are not statistically significant

acceptable.answer: Across American states, polarization in vaccine discussion is strongly negatively correlated with later vaccination rates (r = -0.77). No similar pattern appears in Canada.

spans.text: we confirm a strong negative correlation (r = −0.77, p < 0.001) between vaccine polarization and vaccination rates
We did not observe a similar pattern in Canada

acceptable.note: A supplementary figure caption (page 26, S3 Fig) reports a positive correlation in Canada: 0.74, p = 0.004, n = 12 with Nunavut removed. The abstract calls the Canadian relationship 'notably weaker'. Reporting either the text's wording or the supplementary number is accurate.

acceptable.answer: Polarization spikes coincide with specific political events and announcements and rise and fall within days.

spans.text: many of the largest polarization peaks coincide with highly contentious events specific to each country’s context
These polarization surges typically lasted only a few days

acceptable.decided: Stays secondary: no reviewer restated it, the same rule as F4 in pone.0342063. The labeler asked whether it should be core.

acceptable.answer: Conservative users in both countries posted conspiracy-related material at higher rates. Separately, daily conspiracy tweet volume had a small negative correlation with aggregate daily polarization in the United States (r = -0.247, p = 0.031) and no significant correlation in Canada (r = 0.023, p = 0.831).

spans.text: conservative partisans in both countries tweet conspiracy-related content at higher rates than progressive partisans
we find a small but significant negative correlation for the United States, while no significant correlation was observed for Canada
we find that there is no statistically significant correlation of 0.023 with
including tweets that either promote the conspiracy or debunk / refute it

acceptable.decided: Labeler, 2026-11-21: numbers added. Conspiracy-related tweets include rebuttals, so 'endorsed' overstates (see F-x3). The paper calls the American correlation 'small' on page 21 and 'moderate' on page 22; either word is accepted.

acceptable.answer: Canada showed lower overall measured polarization and a weaker association between regional conservatism and polarization.

spans.text: Canada, while showing similar patterns, demonstrated significantly lower overall polarization levels
We found a similar but much weaker association between polarization and conservative political leaning

acceptable.answer: The pattern has exceptions: liberal Delaware is highly polarized, and conservative Arkansas, Alabama and Idaho are not.

spans.text: Delaware, a liberal state, exhibited unexpectedly high polarization

acceptable.answer: Quebec ranks highest in polarization among Canadian provinces, with the caveat that only English-language tweets were analyzed.

spans.text: Quebec ranks highest overall

rejected.answer: Polarized online discourse lowered vaccination rates.
rejected.why: The paper reports a correlation with rates measured a year later and says it cannot establish causality.

counter_span.text: While we cannot establish causality among conservative voting patterns, polarization scores, and vaccination rates

rejected.answer: The proposed method clearly outperforms existing methods and generalizes robustly.
rejected.why: Reviewer 3 attributed this claim to the manuscript. The authors could not find it and the paper compares against no baseline method. A reviewer's restatement can describe a different paper.

rejected.answer: Conservatives endorsed or believed more conspiracy theories.
rejected.why: Labeler, 2026-11-21: the conspiracy category counts any tweet that discusses a theory, including rebuttals. Reviewer 2 asked how conspiracy tweets were separated from debunking ones; the paper now says they were not.

counter_span.text: including tweets that either promote the conspiracy or debunk / refute it

neutral.answer: The authors suggest that polarized discourse may have helped shape regional vaccination patterns in the United States.
neutral.why: Labeler, 2026-11-21: this is the authors' interpretation of the correlation in F2, prefaced by 'our results suggest' and by a statement that causality cannot be established. Reported as a suggestion it is accurate: no credit beyond F2, no penalty. Reported as a finding that polarized discourse lowered vaccination, it is the rejected F-x1.

spans.text: our results suggest polarized discourse played a significant role in shaping the heterogeneous vaccination landscape across the U.S.

neutral.answer: Republican vote margins had a significant positive effect on polarization about masks and vaccines even after controlling for other factors.
neutral.why: Labeler, 2026-11-21: the discussion says this, but the paper reports correlations only and no analysis with controls. True to the paper's words and unsupported by its results: no credit, no penalty.

spans.text: Republican vote margins had a significant positive effect on polarization in discussions concerning masks and vaccines, even after controlling for other factors

acceptable.answer: Polarization is measured only through semantic similarity of language, a proxy that can miss signals such as sarcasm or indirect disagreement.

spans.text: we measured partisan polarization only through the proxy of semantic similarity

acceptable.answer: Twitter users are more politically engaged and partisan than the public, so the results describe a vocal subset.

spans.text: our results reflect dynamics within a vocal subset of online political discourse

acceptable.answer: User locations come from self-reported profile fields and can be wrong; VPNs, fake accounts and bots add error and may inflate apparent partisan distance.

spans.text: geographic attribution of users depends on self-reported location fields
potentially inflating the apparent semantic distance between political groups

acceptable.answer: The keyword strategies differ between the two countries, which may contribute to the cross-national differences.

spans.text: This asymmetry may have contributed to cross-national differences in patterns of observed polarization

acceptable.answer: The tweets are from late 2020 and the vaccination rates mostly from 2021, so that correlation is suggestive, not causal.

spans.text: should be understood as suggestive rather than causative

acceptable.answer: The analyses are correlational and do not imply causation.

spans.text: these results do not imply causation

acceptable.answer: Only English-language tweets were analyzed, which may bias the Canadian results, Quebec's in particular.

spans.text: we restricted our analysis to English-language tweets

acceptable.answer: In Canada, parties were merged into a left and a right party family, and Bloc Québécois supporters were excluded.

spans.text: we categorized users into liberal (left) and conservative (right) party families

acceptable.answer: Party labels may be inaccurate, because the classification of users into partisan groups relies on self-reported information.

spans.text: our classification into partisan groups relies on self-reported information, which may not be entirely accurate

acceptable.decided: Labeler, 2026-11-21: added, separate from L8. L8 is how parties were grouped; L9 is whether users were put in the right group.

rejected.answer: The authors acknowledge that they report no significance tests or confidence intervals.
rejected.why: Raised by the reviewer whose report does not match the manuscript. The paper reports p-values and confidence intervals.

rejected.answer: The authors list the lack of a comparison with network-based methods as a limitation.
rejected.why: Reviewer 1 asked for the comparison. The paper answers in the introduction by explaining its choice of a text-based method; it is not among the limitations.

counter_span.text: our study adopts a strictly text-based method

acceptable.answer: The paper names no explanatory theory. It positions itself in a methods literature (text-embedding measures of polarization) and in empirical work on partisan responses to the pandemic.
acceptable.decided: Labeler, 2026-11-21: same rule as pone.0342063. Saying that no theory is named earns the bonus; describing the two literatures (T1, T2) is also acceptable.

acceptable.answer: Computational research that measures polarization from text embeddings, as distinct from dictionary-based and network-based approaches.

spans.text: Recent computational approaches increasingly draw on text embedding methods to study polarization

acceptable.answer: Research on partisan divides in responses to the COVID-19 pandemic.

spans.text: This polarization fundamentally shaped how individuals responded to the COVID-19 pandemic

acceptable.answer: Extends: it agrees with earlier findings that right-leaning regions were more divided and adds geographic and temporal resolution.

spans.text: we extended beyond these studies to characterize the geographic heterogeneity and temporal evolution of polarization

rejected.answer: The paper uses a network or echo-chamber approach to polarization.
rejected.why: Reviewer 1 asked for a comparison with network-based work such as Cinelli et al. The paper cites that work and explicitly takes a text-based route instead.

counter_span.text: our study adopts a strictly text-based method

acceptable.answer: Earlier studies: right-leaning states showed greater partisan division over COVID-19 measures. The paper agrees and extends them.

spans.text: we found that more right leaning states and provinces exhibited greater partisan divisions around COVID-19 on Twitter (X)
This main finding is consistent with previous studies suggesting conservative states exhibited higher polarization

acceptable.answer: Prior work: network-based approaches, inferring ideology from follower or retweet structure, are highly effective. The paper sets its text-based method against them because network data has become restricted.

spans.text: network-based approaches such as inferring ideology from follower or retweet structures have proven highly effective in prior work

acceptable.answer: Reference 94: negative sentiment in Canadian vaccine tweets fell during 2020. The paper contrasts its own Canadian result with this.

spans.text: who found reduced negative sentiment in Canadian vaccine-related tweets between January and December 2020

acceptable.answer: Reference 103: Canadians showed a rare cross-partisan consensus on emergency measures early in the pandemic. The paper notes that social media did not mirror it.

spans.text: among Canadians regarding emergency measures in the early stages of the pandemic

acceptable.answer: Prior work: Republican vote share is negatively correlated with vaccination rates. The paper's vaccination result aligns with it.

spans.text: This aligns with the well-documented negative correlation between Republican vote share and vaccination rates

acceptable.answer: Prior work: the language of political discussion varies across socio-demographic groups, each with its own lexicon. The paper takes this as the problem its method must handle.

spans.text: the language of political discussions across socio-demographic groups naturally varies

neutral.answer: Prior research: Democratic supporters were more likely than Republicans to distance, wear masks and get vaccinated. The paper builds on this.

spans.text: Democratic Party supporters were consistently more likely to adhere to social distancing guidelines

neutral.why: Labeler, 2026-11-21: background. The paper does not test compliance and does not set its expectations against this claim. No credit, no penalty.

critical_catches.catch: The abstract says conservative regions were significantly more polarized in both countries; the results report no statistically significant association in Canada.

spans.text: politically conservative regions exhibited significantly higher levels of partisan polarization in both countries
For Canada, these associations are not statistically significant

critical_catches.catch: The abstract calls the link between vaccine polarization and vaccination 'notably weaker' in Canada; the supplementary figure reports a significant positive correlation there (0.74).

spans.text: This relationship was notably weaker in Canada
The correlation is 0.74 with CI = [0.31, 0.92] (n = 12, p = 0.004)

critical_catches.catch: The discussion claims an effect of Republican vote margins 'after controlling for other factors'; the paper reports no analysis with controls.

spans.text: even after controlling for other factors
